reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The xwOBA splits frame the argument immediately: .415 as a hitter, .257 as a pitcher, both 94th percentile or better on their respective sides of the ball. That kind of separation across disciplines doesn't exist anywhere else in the sport. The bat carries a 17.3% barrel rate alongside a 14.6% walk rate, and together they explain a projected .394 OBP and .551 SLG, with the 28.6% whiff rate the one contact cost the discipline and impact consistently offset. On the mound, a 2.69 xERA and 30.4% whiff rate frame a top-of-rotation profile, the 7.6% walk rate the lever that needs to hold for the stuff to fully translate, and if it does, the projected .945 OPS bat and ace-caliber arm coexist exactly the way the Statcast card says they should.

The xwOBA sits at .375 and xSLG at .513, both tracking ahead of what he's actually put up, which means the underlying contact profile is outrunning the surface results rather than the reverse. reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The .430 xwOBA and 22.5% barrel rate are both at the top of the leaderboard, and the 17.2% walk rate makes the plate discipline profile genuinely unusual for someone who also hits the ball that hard. The contact side is the tension: a 31.2% whiff rate means the actual batting average will probably lag behind what the exit velocity suggests he deserves, which is why the xBA sits at .277 while the xSLG is at .612. If he shores up the swing-and-miss even modestly, the projection's .927 OPS looks conservative; if the strikeouts calcify at 29.3%, he's a true-outcome slugger with a fat walk rate and a ceiling that stays intact but a floor that lands closer to his projected .269 average territory. Either way, the power and patience combination at 23 is the kind of profile that ages well.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .307, 99th percentile, and that's where the whole argument starts. Witt's contact quality shows up across the board, 92.9 mph average exit velocity and a 52.2% hard-hit rate, and the 30.3 ft/s sprint speed, also 99th percentile, turns weak contact into hits that would die in other hands. The profile hinges on the chase rate: 33.2% will cost him against pitchers who locate well away, but a 17.5% strikeout rate suggests he makes enough contact on those attempts to keep the damage contained. The projection of .283/.351/.470 with 45 steals doesn't fully capture what the Statcast card is showing; if the chase rate tightens even a little, there's an MVP-caliber season in here.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The 32-homer, 39-steal projection is the kind of line that makes you double-check the name, and the Statcast profile mostly backs it up. His 48.2% hard-hit rate sits in the 85th percentile, and the .359 xwOBA says the quality of contact is pulling real weight, even though his 90.1 mph average exit velocity is only middle-of-the-pack — he's squaring the ball up at an elite rate without being a pure masher. The whole profile hinges on that 35.5% chase rate, which sits in the 18th percentile; if he tightens his zone management even modestly, the 11.2% walk rate compounds and the strikeout damage stays manageable, but if pitchers continue to exploit it, the 26.2% K rate climbs and the batting average bleeds. At 29.5 ft/s sprint speed, the stolen-base ceiling has a clear mechanical basis and the defensive grade follows, so even a partial step forward in plate discipline turns this into a genuine star profile rather than a compelling-but-flawed one.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact-to-power translation is almost absurd: 94.5 mph average exit velocity sitting at the 99th percentile, a 15.2% barrel rate, and an xwOBA of .364 that lines up almost exactly with a projected .838 OPS across 626 PA. The whole profile screams elite bat-to-ball outcomes, except for the strikeout rate. At 27.8%, the whiff problem is real enough that his xBA of .274 trails what the raw power suggests he should hit, and the profile hinges entirely on whether he can sharpen his two-strike decisions without surrendering the aggression that drives the contact quality. If that 28.0% whiff rate drifts down even modestly, you're looking at a legitimate MVP candidate; if it climbs, the 27 home runs and 29 steals projected still make him an elite fantasy asset, but his actual value gets capped somewhere below his ceiling.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.peak_summary: Projection: mid-rotation starter or better with low risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 72.7 AA IP.
reports.published_report: A 1.40 ERA and a 0.70 WHIP across 72.7 AA innings isn't a hot stretch — it's a sustained demolition, and the strikeout-to-walk shape underneath it is what makes the number believable. Anderson has walked 10 batters all year against 108 strikeouts, and the translation puts his BB/9 at 2.1 in MLB context while the league sits at 3.2, so the command isn't a minor-league mirage. The whole percentile stack, ERA, WHIP, BB/9, K-BB%, grades at 99 against his pitcher pool, which means the dominance is broad rather than driven by one inflated rate. Mid-rotation starter is the projection floor; the question is whether the stuff that plays this cleanly at Double-A holds its shape against major-league hitters, and if it does, the ceiling is something considerably better.

reports.name: Eli Willits
reports.peak_summary: Projection: impact everyday bat with medium risk. The current bat shape is impact over 232 A PA.
reports.published_report: The .418 OBP leads the argument, and at 18 it should silence most of the usual caveats about low-A noise. Across A+ & A in 356 PA, Willits is drawing 65 walks against 75 strikeouts, an approach profile that translates to a 12.4% walk rate by MLB equivalency, well clear of the 8.5% MLB average. The ISO sits at .212 in the minors but shaves to .140 in translation, so the hit and walk tool are carrying this profile more than the raw power numbers suggest, and whether he grows into average or better game power is what determines the ceiling. If the approach holds, the projection points to an impact everyday bat two to three years out; if it doesn't, the floor is a reserve.

reports.name: Cristopher Sánchez

reports.name: Nick Kurtz
reports.published_report: The tension in Nick Kurtz's Statcast profile is almost comedically stark: 18.4% walk rate, 36.8% whiff rate, two numbers pulling in exactly opposite directions. His 93.6 mph average exit velocity and 18.1% barrel rate both sit at the 97th percentile, and a 58.3% hard-hit rate that leads essentially the entire league tells you the contact he does make is genuinely punishing. The problem is he's missing a lot of pitches, and a 31.6% strikeout rate means the at-bats where he doesn't walk and doesn't barrel something are often just gone. If he finds even modest contact improvement, the .379 xwOBA and projected .897 OPS become the floor, the walks and the raw power are too loud to suppress, but if the whiff rate holds, he's a weird, valuable player: a first baseman who looks broken on one side of the ledger and elite on the other.

reports.name: Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
reports.published_report: The contact profile is elite, and the power profile is not. Guerrero's 12.9% strikeout rate sits in the top tier league-wide, his .292 xBA reflects genuine bat-to-ball ability, and a 10.9% walk rate means he gets on base at a .361 clip by projection — but a 7.1% barrel rate and xSLG of .416 say the thump that once defined his ceiling has gone mostly quiet. The Statcast picture is a hitter who makes more contact than almost anyone yet doesn't punish mistakes at the rate his raw tools once promised, and a projected 17 home runs across 663 PA is the arithmetic consequence of that mismatch. The whole profile hinges on whether the barrel rate recovers; if it does, the contact foundation turns him back into a middle-of-the-order force, and if it doesn't, he's a high-OBP first baseman who profiles closer to a second-division regular than the star he was supposed to become.

A 93.0 mph average exit velocity sits at the 95th percentile, a 56.0% hard-hit rate is at the 98th, and yet a 36.7% chase rate and 30.6% whiff rate sit at the 13th and 19th percentiles respectively — the raw power is genuine, the swing decisions aren't. The projection absorbs that friction and lands at .258/.318/.457 with 25 home runs across a full season, which is a productive corner outfielder if the strikeouts (28.9%) stay manageable, and something considerably flatter if pitchers learn to live on the edges of his chase zone and he never adjusts. reports.name: Tekoah Roby
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with high risk. The current pitching shape is bat missing over 47 AA IP.
reports.published_report: The command-and-run-prevention profile here is louder than the stuff. Over 47 AA innings, Roby posted a 2.1 BB/9 and a 1.0 WHIP, and the MLB-equivalent translation across AAA & AA turns that control into a 2.7 BB/9, comfortably below what most MLB pitchers allow. The strikeout rate doesn't travel as cleanly; his 10.9 K/9 at AA becomes 8.5 in translation, roughly league average, which tells you the profile runs on location and weak contact more than pure miss. If the command holds at the next level, the floor is a useful relief arm and the ceiling is a starter who survives by keeping the ball on the ground and the bases empty; if the stuff doesn't tick up and the zone control erodes even slightly, what's left is a depth piece.

reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is loud — 12.8 K/9 across AAA & A, translating to 9.2 at the MLB level, and the 35 punchouts in 24.7 innings rank at the 90th percentile against comparable arms. reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with low risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 72.7 AA IP.
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is real enough, the walk rate is the problem. If command tightens, there's a useful arm here; if it doesn't, he's organizational length with a big K/9 that doesn't matter much when he keeps putting men on.

reports.name: Blake Wehunt
reports.peak_summary: Projection: multi-inning or setup reliever with medium risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 53.7 AA IP.
reports.published_report: That K-BB% is the number. At AA this year, Wehunt has struck out 72 batters against just 16 walks across 53.7 innings, and the gap translates to a 16.1% K-BB% in MLB-equivalent terms, well clear of the 13.5% MLB average. The strikeout rate softens in translation, from 12.1 at AA to a projected 9.3 at the big-league level, but the walk rate barely moves, sitting right at the MLB average of 3.2, which means the profile holds its shape rather than depending on a level that inflates misses. The ceiling here is a multi-inning reliever or setup arm, the starter volume across these 53.7 innings notwithstanding, and that's an honest read. If the command holds and the stuff plays in shorter bursts, he's a useful late-game piece; if neither translates, what's left is a depth arm who can eat innings without embarrassing himself.

reports.name: Gary Gill Hill
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with low risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 63.3 AA IP.
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the only part of this profile that isn't a problem. Across AA & A+, Gary Gill Hill's 2.1 BB/9 translates to a 2.7 MLB-equivalent figure, well below what most MLB starters allow, and that command grade of 75 is real enough to keep him in rotation discussions. The trouble is that he misses almost nobody: 71 strikeouts across 90.3 innings produces a 7.1 K/9 that translates to 6.7 at the MLB level, and the K-BB% shrinks from 13% in the minors to 10.5 against big-league hitters. Everything here hinges on whether the command advantage is durable enough to survive without swing-and-miss, because if that walk rate creeps upward even modestly there is no strikeout floor to catch it. The projection ceiling is a back-end starter or late-inning arm with a depth floor, which is an honest read on a 21-year-old who throws strikes but doesn't overpower anyone.

reports.name: Michael Forret
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with high risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 54.3 AA IP.
reports.published_report: The ERA and WHIP are doing most of the talking here, and what they're saying doesn't quite match the strikeout rate. Across AAA & AA this season, Forret's 3.3 ERA and 1.1 WHIP grade in the upper tier of the minor-league pitcher pool, but his K/9 translates to 8.2 at the MLB level, just short of the MLB average of 8.6, and his walk rate translates to 3.8 while the MLB average sits at 3.2. The run-prevention grades 75, the miss and dominance grades 45. That gap is the whole tension in the profile: he's holding hitters down through 79 innings without the strikeout volume to make you feel safe about what happens when the sequencing tightens. If the suppression holds as a real skill and the command shores up enough to protect that 1.1 WHIP in a major-league environment, there's a rotation piece somewhere in there, but the most honest read right now is a depth arm who could stick as a useful arm if the stuff plays up or a reliever if it doesn't.

reports.name: Jonah Cox
reports.peak_summary: Projection: organizational depth with high risk. The current bat shape is impact over 183 AA PA.
reports.published_report: A .400/.453/.644 slash at AA in 183 plate appearances is the kind of line that makes you squint at the park factors before you trust it, and a .464 BABIP gives you every reason to. The translation softens it but doesn't erase it: an MLB-equivalent ISO of .167, strikeouts projecting to 20.8% in the majors where most hitters run north of that, and 27 stolen bases that don't show up in the translation at all. The oblique strain is the read right now, because a left oblique on a right-handed hitter is exactly the injury that can reshape a swing if it lingers, and he's already on the IL retroactive to July 6. If he returns healthy and the contact rate holds anywhere close to what 31 strikeouts in 183 AA PA suggests it can, the ceiling here is a regular; if the BABIP normalizes hard and the oblique nags, the floor is reserve territory, and a 59% projection toward regular-or-better means this profile is genuinely open.
